Apple has filed its response to OpenAI's motion to dismiss the lawsuit that accuses two former employees and OpenAI and io Products of stealing its trade secrets. Here are the details.

A little background

A few days ago, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit Apple had earlier brought against the company, io Products, Chang Liu, and Tang Tan over allegations of trade secret theft.

OpenAI argued in its motion that Apple had filed the lawsuit "without adequate investigation" and went on to present its own version of events in response to Apple's suit.

OpenAI's response is built on three main arguments: that Apple "failed to demonstrate it owns protectable trade secrets," that the company "failed to allege conduct that would reasonably support a misappropriation claim," and that it "failed to reasonably allege any damages or ongoing harm."

OpenAI claims, for example, that contrary to Apple's allegations, former Apple employee Chang Liu was approached by former colleagues for advice after his departure, rather than accessing Apple data without authorisation; as for former Apple vice president Tang Tan, he retained Apple's offboarding documentation in order to help ensure new employees complied with the company's security procedures.

OpenAI also argues that Apple's own information management and offboarding practices are partly to blame, claiming Apple encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts for work and failed to properly cut off their access to company data after they left.

"Apple's complaint is about specific people stealing specific Apple trade secrets in specific ways"

Apple filed its response today, rebutting OpenAI's arguments point by point and stating that "in short, the defendants have failed to meaningfully engage with the core, egregious allegations in the complaint."

Apple argues that its original complaint "sufficiently identified the specific trade secrets misappropriated by defendants," and cites case law noting that courts have found similar levels of detail sufficient to allow trade secret claims to proceed.

Apple also says OpenAI's challenge to Apple's alleged failure to adequately protect its trade secrets is "equally unavailing," and points out that OpenAI "dismisses Apple's trade secrets as mere 'vendor relationships,' then questions whether any 'vendor relationships' qualify as confidential at all."

In its response, Apple also directly addresses a heavily redacted transcript of a conversation that OpenAI published on its website, in which a former colleague still employed at Apple reached out to Chang Liu to clarify some information about an Apple project.

OpenAI argues that the conversation proves Apple was misleading in characterising Liu's post-departure access as theft, because Apple's own employees had asked Liu for help retrieving information.
